comments.author: @MentorofRichandRenegadeWomen
comments.text:
Occurred around the 1950s, the extinction of the Lord Howe Boobook/Owl (Ninox Novaeseelandie albaria). The extinction was triggered by a chain reaction of human-caused ecological disasters.
Human colonisation brought about the clearing and fragmentation of native forests to establish settlements and pastures.
The removal of old trees drastically reduced the natural hollows in tree trunks where these owls nested, leaving surviving populations without safe places to breed.
The Lord Howe Parakeet (Cyanoramphus subflavescens) was also driven to extinction however, unlike the Owl, its disappearance occurred long before.
This bird was wiped directly by the early human settlers.
The last official record of the species dates back to 1869.
The Parakeet, viewed as an agricultural pest, it was hunted, poisoned, and captured en masse by farmers until its total extermination.
The Lord Howe Red-Crowned Parakeet closely resembled the New Zealand Parakeet.
The White-Throated Pigeon (Columba Vitiensis Godmanae) and the Lord Howe Swamphen were also driven to extintion.
The disappearance of both ocurred on the Island (19th century), brought about by the arrival of humans. The last official sighting of the White-Throated Pigeon occurred in 1853.
The Lord Howe Swamphen (Porphyrio Albus): This bird was almost entirely white and unable to fly efficiently. Just like the Pigeon, it lacked any fear of humans, it became the easiest target for ships resupplying on the Island. It was the first bird on the Island to disappear, going extinct around 1834, precisely around the time the first settlers established permanent residency.
